items.title: Gen Z Is Driving Global Political Change, Aiding Far Left and Far Right
items.summary: Protests planned across Europe on Friday are the latest example of global youth anger that has driven demonstrations and election upsets.
items.full_text:
Title: Gen Z Is Driving Global Political Change, Aiding Far Left and Far Right - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/20/world/europe/youth-protests-far-right-left.html

Published Time: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 06:19:26 GMT

Markdown Content:
Thousands of students are poised to hold simultaneous and coordinated protests in several European countries on Friday, demanding an end to war, to social-welfare spending cuts and, in some cases, to capitalism itself.

It is the latest iteration of the global youth uprisings that have spilled through streets from France to India this year, and helped to power recent election upsets across Europe and the Americas.

Polling shows that frustrated young people played a disproportionately large role in voting out nationalist leaders in [Hungary](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/04/13/world/europe/orban-hungary-election-magyar-populism.html) and [Serbia](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/world/europe/serbia-students-vucic-election.html), in electing the first Black senator from [Mississippi](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/elections/voter-trends-mississippi.html) since Reconstruction, and in putting a [German far-right party](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/06/world/europe/germany-afd-saxony-anhalt.html) on track to govern a German state for the first time since World War II. They could prove crucial in upcoming elections in France and Spain.

“It’s becoming harder and harder to not connect all of the different issues facing our generation,” said Adam Powell-Davies, 27, the national chair in Britain of the Socialist Students, one of the groups organizing Friday’s protests. “Not just in specific countries, but globally.”

The beneficiaries of this youth anger are ideologically diffuse. They include centrists — as well as insurgent politicians on the far left and on the far right who offer stark and social-media-friendly solutions to the ailments of an unsettled global order.

Image

Protests in Belgrade, Serbia, in October. A student-led movement helped defeat the country’s nationalist leader in a recent election.Credit...Marko Djurica/Reuters

Organizers and experts say the connective tissue between these spasms of youth anger is a frustration with established political power structures, whatever their ideological bent — and a perception that economic opportunity is slipping away from young people.

A decade of pandemic, war, warming temperatures and a generation-defining fiscal reckoning in wealthy economies have combined to fuel [fears that young people may never enjoy](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/world/youth-aging-europe-pension-ukraine-starshield.html) the peace, prosperity and freedoms of their parents and grandparents. Countries like France are [struggling with high government debt](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/06/world/europe/france-protests-social-welfare-election.html) and face difficult choices for how to maintain the promises of generous social welfare systems.

“There’s no future for us,” Laura Spearey, a 27-year-old information technology student from Bilbao, Spain, who traveled to Britain to join the Friday protests, said in an interview.

She cited difficulties in securing housing, health care and other necessities of adulthood: “You have no chance whatsoever to have your own life, to build your life project _.”_

Those anxieties have persisted for years: They also drove the [“Occupy” protests](https://www.nytimes.com/2011/10/18/us/the-occupy-movements-common-thread-is-anger.html) that followed the 2008 financial crisis. But survey data suggests they are growing more urgent, even in countries, like Germany, where youth unemployment rates are still lower — and there is less government debt — than in Britain and France.

In Germany, young people’s economic concerns have grown in the past decade, according to “Youth in Germany,” an academic study that has surveyed more than 2,000 young people per year over nine years.

“The crucial question is not simply whether today’s young people are objectively worse off than previous generations,” said Klaus Hurrelmann, a professor of public health and education at Berlin’s Hertie School and a co-author of the “Youth in Germany” study. “What matters is that many of them are beginning to believe that the traditional promises of our society no longer apply to them.”

Across much of Europe, that belief has been further fueled by governments’ promises to spend more and more on national defense in the years to come, both to compensate for declining American military support for the continent and to counter threats from Russia. Younger protesters have called for a reversal of that buildup, saying it drains needed money for education, health care and other social services.

In Germany, many protests groups say they have been galvanized by government efforts to encourage young people to sign up for military service in an effort to bolster fighting forces, a move that many young people worry will lead to a military draft.

In a list of demands published ahead of Friday’s protests, one of the German groups organizing the events, “Gen Z Regelt” — roughly translated, “Gen Z Gets Things Done” — called for the resignation of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who has taken the lead in ramping up German military spending. It also says “not one person, not one cent, for the German armed forces.”

Image

A banner reading ‘Gen Z Takes Charge — Time for Resistance’ during a recent youth protest in Wuppertal, Germany.Credit...Matthias Rosenkranz/DPA, via Associated Press 

The group’s demands, like the others behind Friday’s events, skew sharply to the left. They critique the capitalist system. They notably refrain from taking aim at [older generations that have benefited from opportunities](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/world/europe/student-protests-pensions-generations.html) that they fear they are missing out on, like buying homes and securing generous pensions. Instead, they frame the conflict as workers versus the rich and powerful.

“It’s not a battle of the young versus the old,” said Hannah Ponting, 20, a member of the Socialist Students at Liverpool University, who is helping to coordinate protests there. “Neither of those groups are controlling where this money’s going.”

In Berlin in September, similar sentiments — and a surge of voting from people as young as 16 — helped the far-left party Die Linke score an upset victory in the city election.

In other parts of Europe and the world, though, the anxiety has driven young voters [to the far right as well as the left](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/17/world/europe/france-sarre-montangon-protests.html).

According to recent polling in France, roughly [one in five of voters aged under 25](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/17/world/europe/france-sarre-montangon-protests.html) says they will vote for the main far-right party in next year’s election, and [an even higher proportion](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/07/04/world/europe/france-far-right-youth-vote.html) voted far-right in French legislative elections in 2024.

In the German state of Saxony-Anhalt, [exit polls showed](https://www.kas.de/documents/252038/40211523/Wahlanalyse+der+Landtagswahl+in+Sachsen-Anhalt+am+6+September+2026.pdf/85543799-9140-e4a7-ebb1-c195478c3c07?version=1.0&t=1788794826461) the far-right Alternative for Germany party, or AfD, won more than 40 percent of the youngest voters in a state election in September — more than double the share for any other party. The AfD’s main candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, is a telegenic TikTok star who promised to restore opportunity for the state, by deporting some immigrants, providing new benefits to young parents and ending German support for Ukraine.

The success of the AfD and Die Linke in Germany illustrates how quickly young voters are willing to turn on political parties that promised rapid change but failed to deliver, said Mr. Hurrelmann of the Hertie School. Just five years ago, young Germans flocked to centrist parties in a national election.

The centrists have now lost out to the AfD and Die Linke, which have promised radical change by shunning the compromise-driven model of governance that has long dominated German life.

“They are completely free to promise everything,” Mr. Hurrelmann said, “because they are not now in a position to deliver.”

Image

Supporters of Serbia’s student-led movement at their final campaign rally in Belgrade in October. Credit...Mitar Mitrovic/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

Mainstream parties have few incentives to meet young people’s demands, because doing so risks alienating the older voters who make up the majority of their coalitions, said Tim Vlandas, a professor at Oxford University who studies the political consequences of aging populations.

If the far left or far right were to take power, he added, they would likely face similar pressures — because they would also have to appeal to older generations to stay in government.

Such a cycle, he said, would just increase pressure on young people to take to the streets. “When you don’t influence politics, you can protest. You can become alienated and stop voting,” he said. Or, he added, “you can radicalize.”

items.title: A Summit Gives Putin the Win He Craves: Equal Stature With Superpowers
items.summary: Standing alongside the U.S. and Chinese leaders, President Vladimir V. Putin secured a symbolic triumph in his long quest to restore Russia’s place as a global power.
items.full_text:
Title: A Summit Gives Putin the Win He Craves: Equal Stature With Superpowers - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/20/world/europe/putin-trump-xi-summit-apec.html

Published Time: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 08:30:08 GMT

Markdown Content:
President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia stood shoulder to shoulder for the cameras with the leaders of the two global superpowers. He was publicly praised by one of them, President Trump, as “my friend.” And he proclaimed, in between meetings with at least seven world leaders over two days, that efforts to isolate his nation had failed.

Mr. Putin emerged as the big winner after a meeting on Thursday with Mr. Trump and the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, during a summit in Shenzhen, China. The Russian leader walked away with a symbolic triumph in his quarter-century battle to restore Russia’s place as a great power at the fulcrum of world affairs.

Appearing alongside Mr. Trump and Mr. Xi, the two leaders most responsible for helping him escape isolation since his invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Mr. Putin showed that he could be embraced by the powers that matter most without making any compromises on the war.

“It ends the isolation that at least the West tried to impose on him after the full-scale invasion,” said Angela Stent, a Russia expert and senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. “There he is. He is meeting with Xi and Trump, and so much for isolation and sanctions.”

The trilateral meeting — the first of its kind between the three countries — amounted largely to diplomatic theater that elevated Russia beyond its status. Russia lags both the United States and China in economic clout, population size and most other major metrics of influence.

The big exception, apart from landmass and certain natural resources, is nuclear weapons. Russia retains the world’s largest arsenal, an inheritance from the Soviet Union, and Mr. Putin ensured that was not lost on any of the attendees.

Hours before Mr. Putin arrived at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, Russian strategic nuclear bombers landed in Vietnam for the first time since the Soviet era. In Shenzhen, a prominent pro-Putin commentator was filmed incredulously approaching the Russian officer carrying the “cheget,” the nuclear command-and-control device that travels everywhere with the Russian leader, and asking: “Is that the nuclear briefcase, the very one?”

Image

A Russian Tu-95, one of the first nuclear-capable bombers to visit Vietnam since the Cold War, takes off from Da Nang airport on Thursday.Credit...Luu Ngoc Tuan/Associated Press

Mr. Putin had not shown up in person for the annual APEC summit in nine years. The in-person event was canceled from 2019 to 2021. The United States, which played host in 2023, did not invite him because of the war in Ukraine, and an international warrant for his arrest over the transfer of Ukrainian children to Russia complicated visits to Peru and South Korea in 2024 and 2025.

But on Thursday, the Russian leader was granted a place on a red-carpeted stage with his American and Chinese counterparts, even as [he has escalated his war against Ukraine](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/16/world/europe/ukraine-war-life-in-kyiv.html), killing record numbers of Ukrainian civilians and playing hardball during the Trump administration’s renewed efforts to end the conflict.

During the meeting and afterward, the Russian leader and Mr. Trump railed against the International Criminal Court, which [issued](https://www.nytimes.com/live/2023/03/17/world/russia-ukraine-putin-news?smid=url-share#the-international-criminal-court-issues-an-arrest-warrant-for-putin) the arrest warrant for Mr. Putin. Mr. Trump called the institution, which his administration has punished with sanctions, an out-of-control “rogue globalist organization.”

While Russia basked in the diplomatic pomp and pageantry, Ukraine brought a reality check. Just hours before the trilateral meeting, Ukrainian forces for the third time in a week struck the bridge connecting Russia with Crimea, the peninsula that Mr. Putin illegally annexed from Ukraine in 2014.

Image

A satellite image shows the bridge over the Kerch Strait linking Russia and Crimea, that Ukrainian forces have hit three times in a week.Credit...Vantor

Past American presidents have been wary of conferring legitimacy on autocrats actively opposing U.S. interests, but Mr. Trump agreed to the summit with Mr. Putin without forcing any prior commitments regarding Ukraine.

In a news conference afterward, Mr. Putin said he and Mr. Trump shared a common approach to “civilization values” and had a “similarity of views,” citing a recent discussion about democracy.

“What exactly is democracy? What is it?” Mr. Putin asked. “Is it the liberal order that certain circles have sought and are still attempting to impose on the entire world, fashioned according to their own blueprint? Is that democracy or is that a liberal attempt to monopolize power — in fact, liberal dictatorship?”

The formal statement that the three world leaders issued after their meeting made no mention of the conflict in Ukraine, though Mr. Putin and Mr. Trump discussed the topic in talks before the trilateral summit.

During his news conference, Mr. Putin said that, in response to Ukraine’s attacks on the Crimea bridge, he was ruling out any maritime or energy infrastructure truce with Kyiv, and would mete out a painful retaliation.

There had been few signs that such limited cease-fires were in the offing, anyway. At peace talks last week in Abu Dhabi, led by Mr. Trump’s special envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, the Russian negotiating team reissued hard-line [demands](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/us/politics/russia-demand-nato-ukraine.html) from five years before.

Mr. Putin said that, at the insistence of the United States, he had invited European officials to Moscow “through diplomatic channels” to ascertain their position and decide if they should be included in talks. The negotiations up until now have included only the United States, Russia and Ukraine.

Image

Mr. Putin during a news conference in Shenzhen on Thursday.Credit...Pool photo by Maxim Shemetov

Ukraine and European nations have said repeatedly that they must be involved in any discussions about their security. In an interview with NBC News ahead of the summit, President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine said that “big countries always think that they can make decisions about the future of all the world, but it’s a huge mistake, absolutely.”

Mr. Trump and Mr. Putin, however, appear to share the opinion that “there are only a few really serious players” in world affairs that matter, said Ms. Stent, the American Enterprise Institute fellow.

“Trump is obviously a completely different president,” she said. “He is happy to be seen with these authoritarian leaders. He really is not interested in being seen with American allies, either European or Asian.”

Asked whether Thursday’s summit amounted to a new Yalta — the World War II conference where Franklin D. Roosevelt, Winston Churchill and Joseph Stalin brokered the fate of postwar Europe — Mr. Putin replied: “What was so wrong with Yalta?”

He said Yalta finalized the victory over Nazism and paved the way for the United Nations, skipping over how the negotiation set the stage for millions of Europeans to be swept behind the Iron Curtain.

For years, a leading raison d’être of Mr. Putin’s rule has been to reverse the decline of Russian power that came in the aftermath of the Soviet Union’s collapse, which he famously called “the greatest political catastrophe of the century.”

“We showed ourselves to be weak, and the weak get beaten,” Mr. Putin remarked in a 2004 speech after a terrorist attack at a school in Beslan. He seethed with disgust at how vulnerable Russia had become and set the wheels in motion to consolidate domestic political control.

Mr. Putin viewed Moscow’s loss of power as demeaning and humiliating, chafing at the way he was treated as a second-tier leader by American officials. For much of the 1990s and 2000s, U.S. leaders did not regard Moscow as a force to be reckoned with or feared in global affairs.

Over the years, the Russian leader tabulated the slights, growing more intent on ending what he has long called the “unipolar world,” his chosen term for a world he said was unfairly dominated by the United States. Those politics of grievance fueled his increasingly bold and deadly drive to restore Russian might.

Even after Thursday’s summit accorded him the trappings of a superpower leader, Mr. Putin spent part of his news conference saying he was not responsible for invading Ukraine, instead blaming prior Western elites.

“They didn’t give a damn about our opinion, because they believed that there was nothing left to negotiate with Russia. You just have to push,” Mr. Putin said during his news conference on Thursday. “Well, they brought this pressure to the point of hostilities and war.”

items.title: Wreck of First Australian-Built Warship Is Revealed 128 Years After It Sank
items.summary: The wooden gunboat Spitfire was entombed in waters near the Great Barrier Reef after it went down in a cyclone in 1898.
items.full_text:
Title: Wreck of First Australian-Built Warship Is Revealed 128 Years After It Sank - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/20/world/australia/shipwreck-warship-spitfire-great-barrier-reef.html

Published Time: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 08:36:22 GMT

Markdown Content:
Maritime archaeologists and navy divers have located the wreck of the first Australian warship 128 years after it sank, Australia’s Defense Department announced this week.

The authorities and scholars said the discovery of the wooden gunboat, Spitfire, was particularly significant because it was the first warship to be built in Australia in the 1800s under the British colonial government. The ship was constructed in Sydney and launched in 1855. It sank during a cyclone more than 40 years later near the Piper Islands in the Great Barrier Reef.

The wreck site of the 52-foot vessel, made of ironbark and blackwood with copper fastenings, was located in August off the northern state of Queensland after a monthlong expedition that involved a minehunter vessel, remotely operated vehicles and a navy dive team.

An “acoustic anomaly” caused by the wreck was detected by a sonar team, leading to the discovery, the announcement said. Clearance divers with the Australian Navy, specialists who [typically deal with](https://www.navy.gov.au/about-navy/force-commands/mine-warfare-clearance-diving-geospatial-force) underwater demolitions and explosive ordinance removal, then documented the parts of the wreck that were exposed above the seabed, according to maritime archaeologists involved in the search.

Spitfire was commissioned by the state government of New South Wales, where Sydney is located, to protect the city against Russian warships based in Vladivostok, [according to](https://navyhistory.au/spitfire-the-first-australian-built-warship/) the Australian navy. After serving as a patrol boat and pilot vessel, the ship was sold off into private ownership and was used in commercial fishing in the trade for bêche-de-mer, or sea cucumbers.

The site of the wreck is protected as underwater cultural heritage under Australian law.

items.title: Google Disrupts Its Search Advertising With Its Embrace of A.I.
items.summary: The Silicon Valley giant’s search advertising has long fueled the company. But its search ad growth is slowing as A.I. becomes more prevalent.
items.full_text:
Title: Google Disrupts Its Search Advertising With Its Embrace of A.I. - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/19/technology/google-search-ads-ai.html

Published Time: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 09:33:41 GMT

Markdown Content:
Marshall Evans, a marketer who works with small businesses, has helped home repair companies, fitness studios and other mom-and-pop companies buy Google search ads for more than a decade.

The ads — which are tailored to show up when people search on Google for a related term — have been effective in helping a business appear at the top of search results, increasing the chances that someone will click on the ad.

But now those traditional search ads often appear much lower, as Google highlights A.I.-written responses to user queries above its usual list of links and ads.

“A.I. takes over such a large amount of the search results now,” Mr. Evans said.

Mr. Evans’s experience is an example of how A.I. has disrupted Google’s core business of search advertising. As the company plows hundreds of billions of dollars into developing A.I. and incorporating the technology across its services, some longtime advertisers are having second thoughts.

Over the last six months, Mr. Evans, who is based in North Carolina, has moved ad dollars away from Google search ads. For one company that sells trophies, he said, he is allocating $500 a month to the search ads, down from $2,000 a month about a year ago, when Google introduced a feature called A.I. Mode. And he is putting more of the money toward streaming services like Tubi, other search engines like Bing and social media sites like Reddit and Nextdoor.

Last month, Google [reported](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/28/technology/alphabet-earnings-google-ai.html) for the first time that search advertising had fallen to less than 50 percent of its $128 billion in quarterly revenue. Search ad revenue rose 12 percent, falling short of the 15 percent that Wall Street expected.

In effect, A.I. has become a double-edged sword for even the biggest companies. While Google stands to benefit enormously from the technology, including in its booming cloud computing business, A.I. is also taking a toll as the behemoth adjusts to the technology’s effects.

“Google is trying to take a business that was the best business in the world for 10 years and transform it into a different business that doesn’t have the same advantages,” Thomas Monteiro, a senior analyst at Investing.com, said of the move from search to A.I. ads. “Making that transition is a lot harder than Google’s management thought it would be.”

Google’s executives have said the company wanted to make A.I. search features appealing to users, and would think about advertising later. At the top of its search results page, users often now see A.I. Overviews, an A.I.-written answer to the user’s query. The bottom of the summary also invites users to interact with a chatbot through the A.I. Mode feature. Advertising in its A.I. answers and chatbots has not yet taken off.

“We are focused on building the best search user experience, followed by monetization,” Sundar Pichai, Google’s chief executive, said during the earnings call.

Google said users were flocking to its A.I. search tools and that the number of search queries was growing faster than it had in the past five years.

“A.I. is driving an expansionary moment for Search, with our A.I. features leading to increased usage and overall query growth, including commercial queries,” said Thomas Schoenfelder, a Google spokesman. “Our ads experiments have shown promising results and we’re confident about our trajectory.”

Image

Sundar Pichai, the chief executive of Google, last year. “We are focused on building the best search user experience, followed by monetization,” he said during a recent earnings call.Credit...Mike Kai Chen for The New York Times

Advertisers can turn on additional features for the chance to feature their ads in A.I. Mode, which they say cost more money, but there is no guarantee that the promotion will show up. When ads appear in A.I. results, some advertisers say, people are getting caught up in back-and-forth discussions with chatbots instead of clicking their ad and visiting their websites.

“What we’re seeing is arguably the biggest change in searcher behavior,” said Valerie Schlosser, a marketing executive at VML, a global creative agency in New York. Whether people are talking to Google’s chatbot or other chatbots, she said, they are spending more time in conversation and less time surfing the web.

Advertisers aren’t abandoning Google search, she added, but are trying to figure out how to survive in the new system. “Clients are very interested and they want to test new things,” Ms. Schlosser said. “They are interested in ChatGPT and Perplexity, but they are also not totally pulling back from Google.”

Max Anderson, the chief executive of OnlyFinder, a service that helps users find creators on the adult entertainment site OnlyFans, said Google search ads had become more expensive in recent years. He has been running search ads for OnlyFinder on Google since 2022 and ran ads there for his previous company, a software start-up, starting in 2014.

“Our ads won’t show on the page at all, or it will show down the page, below an A.I. Overview,” he said. “Our costs have probably tripled or quadrupled in the last three years.”

The solution was to spend less, he said, adding that he was “gradually and mathematically” pulling back as costs rise and was now devoting about half as much spending to Google ads as he did in the early days of the business. Mr. Anderson declined to discuss specific spending, saying the numbers were proprietary.

Mr. Anderson isn’t planning to abandon Google, but is flummoxed by how to get his business mentioned in A.I. Overviews. Google doesn’t offer advertisers a way to buy guaranteed placement in A.I. Overviews.

“We’d love to have a way as a business to predictably play there, but we have not seen one yet,” Mr. Anderson said.
